html:
Dahomey was a kingdom of the Fon people in what is now southern Benin, from about 1600 to 1904, ruled from Abomey. The map shows it from 1783 to 1900. It is not the Kingdom of Benin, which lay further east in Nigeria; the modern country took the name Benin only in 1975.

Dahomey began on the Abomey plateau inland. King Agaja conquered Allada in 1724 and the port of Ouidah in 1727, giving Dahomey direct access to European ships. It became one of the main sellers of captives in the Atlantic slave trade, taken in wars and yearly raids.

Its army included a corps of women soldiers, the Agojie, whom Europeans called the Dahomey Amazons. The kings held yearly ceremonies, the Annual Customs, with gifts to the people and sacrifices to the royal ancestors.

For much of the 1700s Dahomey paid tribute to the Oyo Empire. King Ghezo ended this around 1823. When Britain pressed it to stop the slave trade, Dahomey turned to selling palm oil. France invaded in 1890 and 1892, defeated King Béhanzin, and made Dahomey part of French West Africa.
